claim: Big+ cells achieve an ~60% faster maximal proliferation rate than naïve cells in the absence of zinc stress in standard rich medium (YPD).
source: Upon closer examination, we noticed that cells harboring the Pus4-induced element also achieved an ~60% faster maximal proliferation rate than naïve cells in the absence of zinc stress in standard rich medium (YPD; Figure 1A, p=0.0095, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with statistical significance (p=0.0095)

claim: In a direct growth competition, Big+ cells outcompete naïve cells with a selection coefficient of nearly 1%.
source: In these experiments, cells harboring Big+ invariably outcompeted the genetically identical naïve cells that lacked it—they live fast—with a selection coefficient of nearly 1% (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental competition data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The fitness advantage conferred by Big+ is larger than those conferred by >30% of non-essential genes.
source: As a frame of reference, the fitness advantage that we measured for Big+ is larger than those conferred by >30% of non-essential genes (Breslow et al., 2008), and the vast majority of natural genetic variants that have been quantified (Jakobson and Jarosz, 2019; Jakobson et al., 2019; Sharon et al., 2018; She and Jarosz, 2018).
evidence: Comparison to published data on fitness effects of gene deletions and natural variants

claim: Big+ cells have progressively lower viability than matched isogenic-naïve controls over the course of 80 days of chronological aging.
source: Over the course of 80 days, Big+ cells had progressively lower viability than matched isogenic-naïve controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by chronological lifespan measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: The median replicative lifespan of Big+ cells is reduced by seven generations compared to naïve cells.
source: These experiments revealed a significant difference in replicative potential between Big+ and naïve cells—the median survival rate is reduced by seven generations (Figure 1D, p<0.0001, Gehan–Breslow–Wilcoxon test, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by replicative lifespan measurements shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance (p<0.0001)

claim: The degree of replicative lifespan shortening in Big+ cells is comparable to that of classic lifespan-altering mutants such as yeast lacking SIR3 or SIR4.
source: This degree of shortening is comparable to that of classic lifespan-altering mutants: yeast lacking SIR3 or SIR4 have reductions of ~3–4 generations, and yeast lacking SIR2 by ~10–11 generations (Kaeberlein et al., 2005; Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: Comparison to published data on lifespan effects of genetic mutations

claim: The growth advantages measured in competition experiments were quantitatively consistent with Monte Carlo simulations sampled from experimental measurements of death rates and growth rates.
source: Notably, the growth advantages we observed in our competition experiment were quantitatively consistent with Monte Carlo simulations sampled from our experimental measurements of the death rates (from chronological lifespan measurements, Figure 2D) and growth rates (from proliferation rate measurements, Figure 2E) of individual cultures in nutrient-starved and replete conditions, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by comparison between experimental data and computational modeling results

claim: During exponential growth, populations of Big+ cells had a similar size distribution to naïve control cells.
source: During exponential growth, populations of Big+ cells had a similar size distribution to naïve control cells.
evidence: Supported by microscopy measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: As cultures became denser, naïve control cells remained the same size whereas isogenic haploid Big+ cells became larger.
source: However, as the cultures became denser, naïve control cells remained the same size whereas isogenic haploid Big+ cells became larger (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy measurements shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The increase in mean area from 22.01 µm2 to 25.36 µm2 in Big+ cells corresponds to a 23% larger volume.
source: This increase in mean area from 22.01 µm2 to 25.36 µm2 corresponds to a 23% larger volume (approximating the yeast cell as a sphere, naïve cell mean radius = 2.65 µm, Big+ cell mean radius = 2.84 µm).
evidence: Calculated from microscopy measurements with geometric approximation

claim: In Big+ cultures 33.1% ± 2.8% of cells exceeded the large cell threshold, whereas 16.5% ± 1.8% did in naïve cultures (p=0.0011).
source: In Big+ cultures 33.1% ± 2.8% of cells exceeded this threshold, whereas 16.5% ± 1.8% did in naïve cultures (p=0.0011 by unpaired t-test; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy measurements shown in Figure 3C with statistical significance (p=0.0011)

claim: The Big+ state does not represent a simple autodiploidization.
source: We therefore conclude that the Big+ state does not represent a simple autodiploidization.
evidence: Supported by mRNA-sequencing data showing expression profiles consistent with haploid mating type Mat a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C)

claim: Diploids resulting from crosses of Big+ cells to naïve cells were significantly larger than those derived from control crosses with two naïve parents.
source: The resulting diploids were significantly larger than those derived from control crosses with two naïve parents (Figure 4A and B), establishing that the trait is dominant.
evidence: Supported by microscopy measurements shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: All cultures derived from the meiotic progeny of Big+× naïve crosses were large.
source: In contrast, all cultures derived from the meiotic progeny of Big+× naïve crosses were large (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy measurements of meiotic progeny shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The non-Mendelian pattern of inheritance of Big+ differs strongly from the expected behavior for genetic mutants or chromatin-based epigenetic elements but is consistent with a prion-based mechanism of transmission.
source: This non-Mendelian pattern of inheritance differs strongly from the expected behavior for genetic mutants or chromatin-based epigenetic elements but is consistent with a prion-based mechanism of transmission.
evidence: Inferred from meiotic inheritance data showing 4:0 segregation pattern

claim: Transient inhibition of Hsp104 did not affect cell size in either naïve or [BIG+] cells.
source: Transient inhibition of the Hsp104 disaggregase, which regulates the inheritance of many amyloid prions (Chernoff et al., 1995; Eaglestone et al., 2000; Halfmann et al., 2012; Shorter and Lindquist, 2004), did not affect cell size in either naïve or [BIG+] cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Transient inhibition of Hsp90 had no impact on [BIG+] transmission.
source: Transient inhibition of the Hsp90 foldase, which regulates the transmission of a different subset of prions (Chakrabortee et al., 2016a), also had no impact on [BIG+] transmission (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Transient inhibition of Hsp70 via expression of a dominant-negative SSA1K69M allele caused [BIG+] cells to lose their large size phenotype permanently.
source: By contrast, transient inhibition of Hsp70 via expression of a dominant-negative SSA1K69M allele (Chakrabortee et al., 2016a; Jarosz et al., 2014; Lagaudriere-Gesbert et al., 2002) caused [BIG+] cells to lose their large size phenotype permanently (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: Propagation of [BIG+] is dependent on the activity of the Hsp70 molecular chaperone.
source: Thus like other prions (Brown and Lindquist, 2009; Chakrabortee et al., 2016a; Chakravarty et al., 2020), and unlike genetic mutations, propagation of [BIG+] is dependent on the activity of this ubiquitous molecular chaperone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Hsp70 dependence and comparison to known prion properties

claim: Hsp70 expression drops dramatically as yeast reach saturation and begin to starve.
source: We note that Hsp70 expression drops dramatically as yeast reach saturation and begin to starve (Werner-Washburne et al., 1989; Werner-Washburne and Craig, 1989) and also decreases as cells age (Janssens et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In naïve cells, Pus4 consistently localized to the nucleolus.
source: In naïve cells, Pus4 consistently localized to the nucleolus, as has been previously reported (Huh et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G and citation to published literature

claim: In [BIG+] cells, the Pus4 protein was present in the nucleolus and also in a fragmented network throughout the cytoplasm.
source: In [BIG+] cells, the Pus4 protein was also present in the nucleolus, but we also observed substantial fluorescence in a fragmented network throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Naïve and [BIG+] strains have equivalent Pus4 protein levels.
source: Using immunoblots to detect the FLAG epitope in naïve and [BIG+] cells, we observed equivalent Pus4 levels, indicating that the phenotypes we observed in [BIG+] cells were not simply due to increased expression of this RNA-modifying enzyme (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: The transfer of [BIG+] cytoplasm into naïve recipient cells resulted in the transfer of the [BIG+] cell size phenotype.
source: The transfer of [BIG+] cytoplasm into naïve recipient cells resulted in the transfer of the [BIG+] cell size phenotype (Figure 4H).
evidence: Supported by cytoduction experimental data shown in Figure 4H

claim: Naïve recipients lacking PUS4 did not acquire the [BIG+] cell size phenotype through cytoduction.
source: However, this was only the case for wild-type recipients. Naïve recipients lacking PUS4 did not acquire the [BIG+] cell size phenotype (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by cytoduction experimental data shown in Figure 4I

claim: Upon PUS4 deletion, the sizes of the mutants derived from naïve and [BIG+] parents were equivalent.
source: We first deleted PUS4 from [BIG+] and naïve cells. Upon PUS4 deletion, the sizes of the mutants derived from naïve and [BIG+] parents were equivalent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: Continuous production of Pus4 is required to maintain the [BIG+] trait.
source: Together with our cytoduction data, this suggested that continuous production of Pus4 is required to maintain this trait.
evidence: Inferred from cytoduction and deletion experiments

claim: PUS4 deletion did not increase the size of naïve cells, suggesting that [BIG+] does not inactivate Pus4.
source: Furthermore, PUS4 deletion did not increase the size of naïve cells, suggesting that [BIG+] does not inactivate Pus4, in contrast to many well-characterized prions that phenocopy loss-of-function alleles of their underlying proteins (Byers and Jarosz, 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and comparison to known prion properties

claim: Even after the re-introduction of PUS4, the size distributions of both populations remained equivalent.
source: Finally, we restored the PUS4 gene to its native locus in these same cells by homology-directed integration. Even after the re-introduction of PUS4, the size distributions of both populations remained equivalent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F

claim: [BIG+] is a protein-based element of inheritance, a prion, formed by the Pus4 pseudouridine synthase.
source: These various lines of evidence—transmission to all meiotic progeny, dependence on molecular chaperones, altered protein localization, and requirement for continuous expression of the protein that initiated the epigenetic trait—lead us to propose that [BIG+] is a protein-based element of inheritance, a prion, formed by the Pus4 pseudouridine synthase.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence including inheritance patterns, chaperone dependence, protein localization, and genetic requirements

claim: Pus4-dependent pseudouridylation of tRNAAGC (Ala) is maintained in [BIG+] cells.
source: Using this approach, we examined the pseudouridylation of an archetypical Pus4 substrate, tRNAAGC (Ala). When a pseudouridine is present and CMC is added, the melting curve shifts relative to an unlabeled control (no CMC). We observed a similar leftward shift in melting curves for both naïve and [BIG+] cells (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR-based pseudouridylation detection data shown in Figure 5B–D

claim: Control cells lacking the Pus4 protein did not produce the melting curve shift indicative of pseudouridylation at U55.
source: In contrast, control cells lacking the Pus4 protein, and therefore lacking pseudouridylation at U55, did not produce this shift (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR-based pseudouridylation detection data shown in Figure 5B–D

claim: Mutations originating at U55 were observed in CMC-labeled samples from both naïve and [BIG+] cells, but not in unlabeled samples or pus4Δ samples.
source: Within the T-arm stem-loop of tRNAAGC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), we saw mutations originating at U55 in CMC-labeled samples from both naïve and [BIG+] cells, but not in unlabeled samples or pus4Δ samples (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Pus4-dependent modification of tRNAs at U55 is maintained in [BIG+] cells.
source: These data establish that Pus4-dependent modification of tRNAs at U55 is maintained in [BIG+] cells.
evidence: Inferred from multiple pseudouridylation detection methods

claim: Only 47 genes changed significantly in expression between naïve and [BIG+] cells (28 decreased and 19 increased).
source: Comparing four replicates each of naïve and [BIG+], the expression levels of only 47 genes changed significantly (28 decreased in expression and 19 increased as estimated using Kallisto and Sleuth; Bray et al., 2016; Pimentel et al., 2017; Benjamini–Hochberg-corrected q-value < 0.05 from the likelihood ratio test and |log2 fold-change| > 1) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by mRNA sequencing data analyzed with statistical methods

claim: The major effects of [BIG+] during exponential growth likely do not occur via changes to steady-state mRNA levels.
source: We conclude that the major effects of [BIG+] during exponential growth (e.g., on growth rate and RLS) likely do not occur via changes to steady-state mRNA levels.
evidence: Inferred from mRNA sequencing data showing minimal changes in transcript levels

claim: No significant differences in bulk tRNA abundance were observed between naïve and [BIG+] cells.
source: We observed no significant differences. While we cannot exclude other effects on tRNA function or the relative abundance of particular tRNAs, our data show that bulk tRNA abundance differences are likely also not responsible for the phenotypes of actively growing cells containing [BIG+].
evidence: Supported by tRNA quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: [BIG+] cells grew nearly twofold better than naïve cells in a sub-inhibitory concentration of cycloheximide (0.01 µg/mL).
source: [BIG+] cells grew nearly twofold better than naïve cells in a sub-inhibitory concentration of cycloheximide that was sufficient to impair proliferation (0.01 µg/mL, in which naïve cells needed 23.6 hours to reach their maximum proliferaton rate vs. 21.3 hours in YPD; for comparison, 100 µg/mL is typically used for experiments that rapidly and completely arrest translation; Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6A

claim: [BIG+] cells proliferated faster in a concentration of rapamycin (10 µM) that inhibited growth.
source: [BIG+] cells also proliferated faster in a concentration of rapamycin (10 µM) that inhibited growth (Figure 6B), suggesting that the pathway may be more active in cells harboring the prion.
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The higher ratio of membrane-localized Par32 observed in [BIG+] cells is consistent with a more active TOR pathway.
source: We found additional evidence in support of this hypothesis by examining the localization of Par32 (phosphorylated after rapamycin 32); the higher ratio of membrane-localized Par32 that we observed in [BIG+] cells is consistent with a more active TOR pathway (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; Varlakhanova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and citation to published literature

claim: Loss of TOR pathway function is associated with extended lifespan in yeast and many other organisms including nematodes, fruit flies, and mice.
source: These latter observations also provide a potential explanation for the decreased longevity of [BIG+] cells: loss of TOR pathway function is associated with extended lifespan in yeast (Dikicioglu et al., 2018; Fabrizio et al., 2001; Powers et al., 2006) and many other organisms including nematodes, fruit flies, and mice (Bjedov et al., 2010; Harrison et al., 2009; Robida-Stubbs et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: When grown in cycloheximide or rapamycin to saturation, [BIG+] cells were no longer large compared to naïve controls.
source: When grown in cycloheximide or rapamycin to saturation, [BIG+] cells were no longer large compared to naïve controls (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and D

claim: Unperturbed translation is necessary for the increased size of [BIG+] cells.
source: Thus, unperturbed translation is necessary for the increased size of [BIG+] cells.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing loss of large cell phenotype during translation inhibition

claim: Populations derived from [BIG+] ancestors were once again significantly larger than naïve controls after recovery from cycloheximide or rapamycin treatment.
source: We then examined their size distributions. Populations derived from [BIG+] ancestors were once again significantly larger than naïve controls that we subjected to the same propagation regime (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6C and D

claim: [BIG+] depends on protein synthesis to augment cell size but the prion is stable to transient perturbations in translation.
source: We conclude that [BIG+] depends on protein synthesis to augment cell size but that the prion is stable to transient perturbations in translation.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing reversible loss of large cell phenotype during translation inhibition

claim: Translation is rate-limiting for growth in nutrient-rich conditions.
source: Translation is rate-limiting for growth in nutrient-rich conditions (Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In synthetic defined medium with identical carbon source abundance but fewer amino acids, nucleosides, and other nutrients, [BIG+] cells did not grow faster than naïve controls.
source: However, in synthetic defined medium with identical carbon source abundance (2% glucose) but fewer amino acids, nucleosides, and other nutrients for optimum growth (SD-CSM), [BIG+] cells did not grow faster than naïve controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: The firefly reporter with normal codons did not produce more luciferase activity in [BIG+] cells than in naïve cells.
source: The firefly reporter with normal codons did not produce more luciferase activity in [BIG+] cells than in naïve cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E

claim: The firefly reporter with rarer codons produced normalized luciferase levels approximately 50% higher in [BIG+] cells than in isogenic naïve control cells.
source: However, the firefly reporter with rarer codons produced normalized luciferase levels approximately 50% higher in [BIG+] cells than in isogenic naïve control cells (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6E

claim: [BIG+] cells may enhance the translation of some mRNAs, especially those containing a greater frequency of rare codons.
source: These data suggest that [BIG+] cells may enhance the translation of some mRNAs, especially those containing a greater frequency of rare codons.
evidence: Inferred from luciferase reporter assay data

claim: More total protein per cell was reproducibly obtained from [BIG+] cultures compared to naïve cultures.
source: We next investigated whether [BIG+] had global effects on the proteome by isolating total protein from cells harboring the prion and naïve controls. We reproducibly obtained more total protein per cell from the [BIG+] cultures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by protein quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D

claim: [BIG+] does not exert substantial changes on the relative levels of the most highly expressed proteins.
source: Coomassie staining of these gels showed no pronounced differences in banding patterns (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that [BIG+] does not exert substantial changes on the relative levels of the most highly expressed proteins, which are known to be efficiently translated (Gingold and Pilpel, 2011; Plotkin and Kudla, 2011).
evidence: Supported by gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and citations to published literature

claim: Polysomes were increased in [BIG+] cells relative to naïve controls, with the polysome-to-monosome ratio increasing from ~2.9 to 3.2.
source: However, polysomes—which are responsible for most protein synthesis (Noll, 2008; Warner and Knopf, 2002)—were increased in [BIG+] cells relative to naïve controls, with the polysome-to-monosome ratio increasing from ~2.9 to 3.2 (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 6F and citations to published literature

claim: The rate of newly synthesized total protein was higher in [BIG+] cells (10,179 cpm/min) compared to naïve cells (8812 cpm/min).
source: These experiments established that the rate of newly synthesized total protein was higher in [BIG+] cells (10,179 cpm/min) compared to naïve cells (8812 cpm/min) (Figure 6G; p<0.0011, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by [35S]-methionine pulse labeling data shown in Figure 6G with statistical significance (p<0.0011)

claim: [BIG+] cells have a higher translation rate, which can increase total protein output, including the levels of some proteins translated from mRNAs enriched with codons generally associated with lower translation efficiency.
source: In summary, we found that [BIG+] cells have a higher translation rate, which can increase total protein output, including the levels of some proteins translated from mRNAs enriched with codons generally associated with lower translation efficiency.
evidence: Inferred from multiple translation measurements including polysome profiling and pulse labeling

claim: For naïve cells, 36.2% were in G1, whereas only 27.2% of [BIG+] cells were in G1, a ~25% reduction.
source: For naïve cells, 36.2% were in G1, whereas only 27.2% of [BIG+] cells were in G1, a ~25% reduction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F, p=0.0017, unpaired t-test).
evidence: Supported by cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F with statistical significance (p=0.0017)

claim: A shortened G1 stage in [BIG+] cells is consistent with their increased protein synthesis.
source: These data suggest that the cell cycle checkpoint for progression to S phase remains intact, and that a shortened G1 stage in [BIG+] cells is consistent with their increased protein synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from cell cycle analysis and translation measurements

claim: [BIG+] cells are not larger during exponential phase growth, suggesting that their cell size checkpoint remains intact.
source: [BIG+] cells are not larger during exponential phase growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that their cell size checkpoint remains intact.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Cells in stationary phase may continue to accumulate mass at a faster rate, contributing to their larger size.
source: By contrast, cells in stationary phase, which do not have the nutrient content needed to progress to S phase, may continue to accumulate mass at a faster rate, contributing to their larger size.
evidence: Speculative inference based on cell cycle and growth data

claim: In [BIG+] cells, seven proteins were increased, one was decreased, and five remained similar in 2-D gel electrophoresis of pulse-labeled proteins.
source: We also analyzed the [35S]-methionine signal from 13 proteins that we could separate by 2-D gel electrophoresis. In [BIG+] cells, seven were increased, one was decreased, and five remained similar (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: Supported by 2-D gel electrophoresis data shown in Figure 6H and I

claim: [BIG+] cells have an altered translation program, with variations in even the most rapidly synthesized proteins.
source: These data suggest that [BIG+] cells have an altered translation program, with variations in even the most rapidly synthesized proteins.
evidence: Inferred from 2-D gel electrophoresis data

claim: Of the 4233 fusions whose abundance could be robustly quantified, ~130 were differentially expressed in [BIG+] cells (81 upregulated and 46 downregulated).
source: Of the 4233 fusions whose abundance could be robustly quantified across the four replicates (Z-score < 1 for both naïve and [BIG+]), ~130 were differentially expressed in [BIG+] cells. Consistent with a bias toward enhanced translation, 81 were upregulated and 46 were downregulated (Figure 6J and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide GFP fusion screen data shown in Figure 6J and Supplementary file 3

claim: Proteins that were increased in [BIG+] cells had a modest decrease in their codon adaptation index (CAI) at the 5' end of their mRNAs relative to all genes.
source: We did, however, observe that proteins that were increased in [BIG+] cells had a modest decrease in their codon adaptation index (CAI) at the 5' end of their mRNAs relative to all genes (Figure 6K), indicating that cells harboring the prion might more efficiently translate these messages.
evidence: Supported by codon adaptation index analysis shown in Figure 6K

claim: The 81 upregulated proteins included multiple ORFs whose deletions are associated with decreased cell size.
source: The 81 upregulated proteins included multiple ORFs whose deletions are associated with decreased cell size (such as PHO5, MRPS28, KAP122, and SWE1; Harvey and Kellogg, 2003; Jorgensen et al., 2002), increased chronological lifespan (DIG2 and UBX6; Garay et al., 2014), and extended RLS (ENO1, MUB1, PHO87, PGM2, and YRO2; McCormick et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by GFP fusion screen data and citations to published literature on gene functions

claim: The 46 downregulated proteins included ORFs whose deletions are associated with increased cell size and decreased chronological lifespan.
source: Conversely, the 46 downregulated proteins included ORFs whose deletions are associated with increased cell size (RNR4 and RPL15B; Jorgensen et al., 2002; Perlstein et al., 2005) and decreased chronological lifespan (including BUD23, SMI1, MHP1, and CLG1; Garay et al., 2014; Marek and Korona, 2013).
evidence: Supported by GFP fusion screen data and citations to published literature on gene functions

claim: Several proteins directly involved in translation control and ribosome biogenesis were increased in [BIG+] cells, including FHL1, MRPS28, MRPS16, RPL24B, RPS7A, and UTP10.
source: Several proteins directly involved in translation control and ribosome biogenesis were also increased in [BIG+] cells, including FHL1, MRPS28, MRPS16, RPL24B, RPS7A, and UTP10 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by GFP fusion screen data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G

claim: The [BIG+]-regulated proteins included 29 ORFs associated with differential sensitivity to rapamycin and 14 ORFs that are known genetic or physical interactors with TOR1.
source: The [BIG+]-regulated proteins also included 29 ORFs associated with differential sensitivity to rapamycin (including SAS4, SNF1, and HCA4; Butcher et al., 2006; Dudley et al., 2005; Kapitzky et al., 2010) and 14 ORFs that are known genetic or physical interactors with TOR1 (including GCD14 and PAR32; Krogan et al., 2006; Varlakhanova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by GFP fusion screen data and citations to published literature on gene functions and interactions

claim: The phenotypes of [BIG+] are likely derived from an altered translational regulation program that favors increased cell size and proliferation at the expense of lifespan.
source: The functional breadth of these effects on the proteome and their logical connection to factors involved in the control of proliferation, cell size, and lifespan suggest that the phenotypes of [BIG+] are likely derived from an altered translational regulation program that favors increased cell size and proliferation at the expense of lifespan.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence including proteome-wide screen and functional analysis

claim: TEF1/TEF2 position U239 is robustly pseudouridylated in a Pus4-dependent manner.
source: The best-documented mRNA target of Pus4 is the translation elongation factor TEF1/TEF2—whose position U239 is robustly pseudouridylated in a Pus4-dependent manner (Carlile et al., 2014; Lovejoy et al., 2014; Schwartz et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TEF1/TEF2 U239 was pseudouridylated in both naïve and [BIG+] cells, in contrast to very low/background levels in pus4Δ cells.
source: We observed TEF1/TEF2 U239 pseudouridylation in both naïve and [BIG+] cells, in contrast to very low/background levels in pus4Δ cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by CLAP method data shown in Figure 7B

claim: TEF1/TEF2 was pseudouridylated in wild-type cells (both naïve and [BIG+]) in a Pus4-dependent manner.
source: Finally, using the aforementioned qPCR-based method for detecting pseudouridylation (Figure 5A), we found additional evidence that TEF1/TEF2 was pseudouridylated in our wild-type cells (both naïve and [BIG+]) in a Pus4-dependent manner (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR-based pseudouridylation detection data shown in Figure 7C

claim: An increase in the signal of pseudouridylation in [BIG+] cells relative to naïve was observed for TEF1/TEF2 mRNA.
source: By quantifying differences in the melt curve shift after CMC labeling—an analysis made simpler for TEF1/TEF2 than for tRNAs by the absence of other pseudouridylated positions flanking U239—we observed an increase in the signal of pseudouridylation in [BIG+] cells relative to naïve (Figure 7D and E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by high-resolution melting curve analysis data shown in Figure 7D and E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: The catalytic function of Pus4 is retained in [BIG+] cells and may be enhanced for specific substrates.
source: Together these data demonstrate that the catalytic function of Pus4 is retained in [BIG+] cells and may be enhanced for specific substrates, contrasting with the classical view of prions as being loss-of-function protein conformations.
evidence: Inferred from pseudouridylation measurements showing maintained or increased activity

claim: 20% (four isolates out of twenty) of wild S. cerevisiae strains became smaller after transient Hsp70 inhibition.
source: We measured the size of cells before and after this chaperone curing and found that 20% (four isolates out of twenty)—'273614N' (clinical, Newcastle, UK); 'L-1528' (fermentation, Cauquenes, Chile); 'DBVPG1373' (soil, Netherlands); 'BC187' (barrel fermentation, Napa Valley, California)—became smaller after curing (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data from wild yeast strains shown in Figure 8A

claim: Two of the four wild isolates that became smaller upon curing showed significant changes to translation.
source: Two of the four isolates showed significant changes to translation (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 8B

claim: BC187 yielded the largest change upon curing, an ~40% reduction in the translation of a firefly luciferase containing a 'normal' suite of codons.
source: BC187 yielded the largest change upon curing, an ~40% reduction in the translation of a firefly luciferase containing a 'normal' suite of codons, similar in magnitude to what we had observed with [BIG+] cells generated in the laboratory.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 8B

claim: In uncured BC187 cells, Pus4 was observed in a fragmented network throughout the cytoplasm, similar to laboratory [BIG+] cells.
source: In uncured cells, we observed Pus4 in a fragmented network throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 8C), similar to what we observed in laboratory [BIG+] cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8C

claim: In cured BC187 cells, the Pus4 signal was more diffuse.
source: In contrast, in cured BC187 cells, the signal was more diffuse.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8C

claim: Cured BC187 cells treated with transient overexpression of Pus4 protein became large.
source: Indeed, cured BC187 cells treated in this way became large (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8D

claim: Transient overexpression of Pus4 did not increase the size of the already-large BC187 natural isolate.
source: By contrast, transient overexpression of Pus4 did not increase the size of the already-large BC187 natural isolate (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Epigenetic and potentially Pus4 prion-mediated control of mechanisms like [BIG+] is likely present in nature.
source: Together, these observations suggest that epigenetic and potentially Pus4 prion-mediated control of mechanisms like [BIG+] that we have described in the laboratory is also likely present in nature.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with wild yeast strains showing similar phenotypes and Pus4 dependence

claim: An enzyme that catalyzes the epigenetic modification of RNA can itself be controlled by an extrachromosomal epigenetic process: a self-templating protein conformation that persists over long biological timescales.
source: Here we show that an enzyme that catalyzes the epigenetic modification of RNA can itself be controlled by an extrachromosomal epigenetic process: a self-templating protein conformation that persists over long biological timescales.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing prion-based control of Pus4 activity

claim: Prion cells not only maintain pseudouridylation activity but that activity can be increased, even without any detectable increase in PUS4 expression.
source: We found that prion cells not only maintain pseudouridylation activity but that activity can be increased, even without any detectable increase in PUS4 expression.
evidence: Supported by pseudouridylation measurements and protein expression data

claim: Changes to the translational control of numerous genes are logically connected to the [BIG+] phenotypes.
source: Instead, we found that changes to the translational control of numerous genes are logically connected to these phenotypes. These include genes that affect cell size, chronological lifespan and replicative lifespan, translation control and ribosome biogenesis, and differential sensitivity to rapamycin (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Inferred from proteome-wide screen and functional analysis

claim: Translation is a rate-limiting step for growth in many organisms.
source: Translation is a rate-limiting step for growth in many organisms (Polymenis and Schmidt, 1997; Sonenberg, 1993) and is often activated in human cancers (Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Other prions in yeast also affect translation, including [PSI+] and [MOD+].
source: Other prions in yeast also affect translation, including [PSI+] and [MOD+] (Baudin-Baillieu et al., 2014; Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In contrast to [BIG+], [PSI+] and [MOD+] lead to losses of their underlying protein activities, impairing translation and growth in many conditions.
source: However, in contrast to [BIG+], they lead to losses of their underlying protein activities, impairing translation and, in turn, growth in many conditions (Baudin-Baillieu et al., 2014; Cox, 1965; Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In [BIG+] cells, translation appears to be amplified—it is faster, leading to higher expression levels of many proteins.
source: In contrast, in [BIG+] cells, translation appears to be amplified—it is faster, leading to higher expression levels of many proteins.
evidence: Inferred from multiple translation measurements

claim: Translation is coupled to cell size, proliferation, and lifespan.
source: Translation is also coupled to cell size, proliferation, and lifespan (Ecker and Schaechter, 1963; Kaeberlein and Kennedy, 2007; Lloyd, 2013; Steffen and Dillin, 2016; Tanenbaum et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Cell size is determined in large part by the activity of the TOR pathway.
source: Cell size, which is determined in large part by the activity of the TOR pathway (Fingar et al., 2002; Zhang et al., 2000), has been inversely correlated with lifespan (Anzi et al., 2018; He et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2011), and older cells are larger (Egilmez et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Molecules that extend lifespan, such as rapamycin, also influence cell size and proliferation by restricting the cell's translation capacity.
source: Moreover, molecules that extend lifespan, such as rapamycin, also influence cell size and proliferation by restricting the cell's translation capacity (Beretta et al., 1996; Terada et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: [BIG+] provides an epigenetic paradigm that links translation, cell size, proliferation, and lifespan.
source: Here we describe an epigenetic paradigm that links all of these fundamental cellular properties: translation, cell size, proliferation, and lifespan.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: The aging defect of [BIG+] cells is likely due at least in part to pleiotropic consequences of their increased proliferation and translation capacity.
source: At present, we favor a hypothesis in which the aging defect of [BIG+] cells is due at least in part to pleiotropic consequences of their increased proliferation and translation capacity.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental data and known relationships between translation, proliferation, and aging

claim: The replicative lifespan of wild budding yeast strains varies widely.
source: The replicative lifespan of wild budding yeast strains varies widely (Kaya et al., 2015) and has been associated with changes in oxidative phosphorylation, respiration, and differences in metabolite biosynthesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Prior studies have characterized genetic links between cell size and lifespan in yeast—mutants that make cells larger tend to age faster, and older cells tend to be larger than younger cells.
source: We note that prior studies have characterized genetic links between cell size and lifespan in yeast—mutants that make cells larger tend to age faster, and older cells tend to be larger than younger cells (Neurohr et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2011; Zadrag-Tecza et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: [BIG+] provides an epigenetic mechanism to alter the relationships between cell size and lifespan heritably.
source: [BIG+] provides an epigenetic mechanism to alter these relationships heritably.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing heritable changes in cell size and lifespan

claim: Exerting epigenetic, rather than genetic, control over basic cell growth behaviors could be valuable in the face of fluctuations between nutrient-replete and nutrient-poor conditions.
source: Exerting epigenetic, rather than genetic, control over basic cell growth behaviors could be valuable in the face of fluctuations between nutrient-replete and nutrient-poor conditions.
evidence: Speculative inference based on modeling and experimental data

claim: Theory predicts that epigenetic mechanisms can have substantial adaptive value when the frequency of environmental fluctuations is rare relative to the frequency of phenotypic change.
source: Theory predicts that such mechanisms can have substantial adaptive value when the frequency of environmental fluctuations is rare relative to the frequency of phenotypic change (King and Masel, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Conditions in which the prion confers a growth benefit match those that promote its propagation.
source: Conditions in which the prion confers a growth benefit match those that promote its propagation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on growth conditions and chaperone expression

claim: Conditions in which the prion is detrimental, shortening lifespan, are also known to reduce chaperone expression and could thereby cure the prion.
source: Conversely, conditions in which the prion is detrimental, shortening lifespan, are also known to reduce chaperone expression (Janssens et al., 2015; Werner-Washburne et al., 1989; Werner-Washburne and Craig, 1989) and could thereby cure the prion.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and citations to published literature on chaperone expression

claim: The strong dependence of [BIG+] on chaperones means that it is a natural epigenetic sensor of its environment.
source: The strong dependence of [BIG+] on chaperones therefore means that it is a natural epigenetic sensor of its environment.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on chaperone dependence and environmental conditions

claim: Cancer cells experience frequent oscillations in their environments as tumors grow and metastasize, with cells exposed to shifting gradients of oxygen and glucose that influence their proliferation rate.
source: Indeed, cancer cells also experience frequent oscillations in their environments: as tumors grow and metastasize, cells are exposed to shifting gradients of oxygen and glucose that influence their proliferation rate (Martinez-Outschoorn et al., 2017; Schito and Semenza, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Multiple lines of evidence suggest that translational hyperactivation can fuel pathological proliferation.
source: However, multiple lines of evidence suggest that translational hyperactivation can also fuel pathological proliferation (Robichaud et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature
